summary:
Amapá stands under Brazil's national framework, and no state-level deviation affecting a visitor is documented in the sources. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since the National Council of Justice resolution of 14 May 2013, adopted 14-1, and joint adoption has been available since 2010 with full rights from 2015. Legal gender change has required no surgery, hormones or diagnosis since the Supreme Federal Court ruling of 1 March 2018, and gender-marker change proceeds by self-determination.

On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court held that discrimination and violence on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity constitutes a crime equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989, docketed as ADO 26 and MI 4733, carrying imprisonment of one to five years and fines. That ruling is the operative basis on which homophobia and transphobia are treated as criminal conduct, and an expat legal guide confirms that same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules operate nationwide, so a trans visitor's status and documents are handled on the same footing as anyone else's at entry.

Documents remain binary. There is no third-gender option in national identity documents, although civil-registry entries recording 'non-binary/unspecified' have been possible since 2020, and a Superior Court of Justice ruling of 6 May 2025 permits rectification of registry entries to a neutral gender and stands as precedent for further cases.

The protective text does not describe what people routinely encounter. Outright International's country overview records that Brazil retains one of the world's highest rates of violence against sexual and gender minorities, particularly trans people, and that these advances face repeal pressure in a conservative Congress. Enforcement of the anti-discrimination provisions is uneven in practice, and smaller cities and rural areas may present more social friction despite identical legal rights, a factor that bears on a visitor moving through Amapá's less urbanised territory.
tangentialFactors:
Political visibility of trans people has risen sharply. The country's first transgender federal legislators, Erika Hilton and Duda Salabert, were elected in 2022, and more than 3,000 openly LGBTQ candidates ran in the 2024 municipal elections, indicating local-level presence of openly trans and LGBTQ office-seekers.

Brazil's protections are described in legal commentary as among the most progressive in Latin America on paper: same-sex marriage under National Council of Justice Resolution 175/2013, joint adoption, name and gender-marker change without surgery, and homophobia and transphobia criminalised as equivalent to racism. The same commentary stresses that enforcement lags the statutory text, which is the gap a visitor is most likely to notice.
localsOnly:
Gender-marker change proceeds by self-determination for residents, and trans voters may register to vote under their lived name and identity even before their identity documents have been updated.

Residents have access to joint adoption and to the full range of family rights attached to same-sex marriage, and the Superior Court of Justice ruling of 6 May 2025 gives a route to rectify a civil-registry entry to a neutral gender where no third-gender marker exists on identity documents.

Residents also live under the repeal pressure noted in the sources: legislative advances can be rolled back by the conservative Congress, and the practical protection available depends on enforcement by prosecutors and police rather than on the statutory text alone.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Amapá-specific source in the inventory documents state-level legislation, police conduct, hate-crime incidents, detention placement or access to gender-affirming care within the state; whether Amapá's own security and health services follow the national framework in practice is unresolved on this inventory.

Whether civil registries in Amapá have in practice issued 'non-binary/unspecified' entries since 2020, and how readily the 6 May 2025 neutral-gender rectification precedent has been applied in the state, are not sourced here.

The inventory gives no figures for violence against trans people in the North of the country or in Amapá specifically; the national rates cited are country-level and are not broken down by state.
